new_statements.quote: Der dynamische Akzent wird durch den Acutus ' ausgedrückt. Sehr häufig fällt er auf die drittletzte Silbe, weshalb in dem Falle von einer Bezeichnung des Akzents abgesehen ist. new_statements.translation: The dynamic accent is expressed by the acute '. Very often it falls on the antepenultimate syllable, for which reason in that case the marking of the accent is dispensed with. [...] If the accent falls on the first syllable of a disyllabic word, it is likewise not marked. Enclitic words are joined by — to the word they belong to, onto which they throw the accent. Some words have two peaks, but no special marking for the second accent is used. The accentuation sometimes fluctuates in the same words.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's Gordon record (antepenultimate stress = antepenultimate) as the most frequent position, and adds that it is a tendency with fluctuation, enclitic shift and occasional double peaks. Preuss's material is from Jesús María and San Francisco (El Nayar), i.e. the catalog's variety.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (a dynamic, not pitch, accent) most often falls on the antepenultimate syllable; that is the unmarked default in Preuss's transcription (disyllables default to initial stress). Enclitics shift the accent onto the host word; the dictionary (line 46014ff.) marks the accent on headwords only where the word is independent or prefixes do not change it, again treating the antepenult as the usual place.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Manche Worte sind zweigipflich' — some words have two accent peaks, but Preuss does not mark the second one.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent is only 'very often' antepenultimate, not always; enclitics attract the accent; accentuation fluctuates between tokens of the same word; when the accent and the saltillo (glottal stop) fall on the same vowel, either half of the vowel may carry it.
new_statements.identity_note: Jáuregui 2025 (not opened) describes Tereseño (Santa Teresa) Cora, a different Cora variety from El Nayar Cora elna1235 (the the compilation's maps it to sant1424; unverified). Preuss 1912 covers Jesús María and San Francisco (El Nayar); Kim & Valdovinos 2014 cover Jesús María ('Mariteco') Cora only, two speakers, words in isolation.

new_statements.relation_note: Contradicts the catalog's fixed: antepenultimate syllable record in kind: it characterises Cora stress as lexical (roughly half of monomorphemic disyllables are final-stressed, which a fixed antepenult/leftward rule would not predict) rather than positionally fixed. The two are not strictly incompatible, since the catalog's pattern string only specifies 3+ syllable words and K&V only examined 1-2 syllable words, but K&V give no positional rule and use 'lexical stress' throughout. Variety: Jesús María (Mariteco), El Nayar, i.e. within elna1235.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mariteco (Jesús María) Cora has lexical stress, cued by high pitch on the stressed syllable and devoicing of final unstressed vowels; monomorphemic disyllables are stressed either initially or finally (24+4 initial vs 22 final for one speaker, 25+5 initial vs 37 final for the other, table (12) p. 7), so position is not predictable from syllable count; the definite-article prefix ɨ́- attracts stress off the noun. The paper argues there is no tone contrast independent of laryngealization, i.e. no tonal system beyond stress (against Casad n.d.).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shift under the stress-attracting definite article prefix; the data are words in isolation only, mono- and disyllables (longer words excluded), two speakers.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (Gordon) records Cora as fixed quantity-insensitive antepenultimate stress (100/0100/00100..). Casad instead describes a phonemic tone system with lexically and morphologically determined high-tone placement, mentions stress only as having primary/secondary degrees partly independent of tone, and gives no synchronic fixed stress position (penultimate stress is cited only as a historical source of tone shifts). That is a different prosodic type from the catalog's fixed antepenult; it neither states nor supports an antepenultimate rule. Dialect note: Casad's data are from Jesús María (El Nayar = elna1235), whereas McMahon 1967 (the likely basis of Gordon's entry) used Presidio de…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Casad analyses Jesús María (El Nayar) Cora as having phonemic (high vs non-high) tone and contrastive vowel length; stress exists in primary and secondary degrees and is 'partly independent' of tone, but no rule for where stress falls is given. High-tone placement is lexical and morphologically mobile (tone attraction to articles/DISTR, singular~plural tone shift in animate nouns, tense/aspect-conditioned placement on 'mobile stress' verb stems); a penultimate stress rule is invoked only as a historical (earlier-stage) explanation for some tone shifts.
new_statements.secondary_stress: States only that stress 'can be analyzed into primary and secondary degrees' (p.157); no placement rule for either degree.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone attraction: nouns lose their single high tone after a preposed article, locative particle or distributive tyi'- (p.167); animate-noun classes with singular/plural tone shift (pp.167, 227); 'mobile stress' verb stems whose high tone moves to prefixes (subject, distributive, completive wa-, perfective ta-, ablative a-, directional uu-) or sits stem-finally/on suffixes by tense-aspect (pp.304-306); word-final high tone sometimes from final-syllable truncation (p.305).
new_statements.identity_note: Casad 1984 explicitly describes the El Nayar dialect spoken in Jesús María and rancherías south along the Río Jesús María (p.155) = elna1235 proper. Jáuregui 2025 (not opened) is by title a sketch of Tereseño (Santa Teresa) Cora, i.e. the Dolores/Santa Teresa dialect area (Glottolog sant1424 / ISO cok), not Jesús María Cora. McMahon 1967, the probable basis of the catalog's Gordon entry, is based on Presidio de los Reyes / San Pedro Ixcatán speakers per Casad p.155.

tone_statements.quote: Fonológicamente, el tañíuka es una lengua muy compleja que cuenta con tono, acento, vocales modales breves y largas, así como con vocales asociadas a rasgos glotales que desencadenan diversos tipos de fonación (Casad 2012, Kim, Y. y M. tone_statements.translation: Phonologically, Tañíuka [Cora] is a very complex language that has tone, stress, short and long modal vowels, as well as vowels associated with glottal features that trigger various phonation types (Casad 2012; Kim & Valdovinos 2015). To date there is still no phonetically based reference phonology that has convincingly established the phonemic status of all these tonal and metrical phenomena in any variety of Náyeeri, nor an analogous study of the allophones of the segmental inventory, nor a work that has disentangled the main morphophonemic processes of the language.

tone_statements.summary: Cora has both tone and stress (with vowel length and glottalized-vowel phonation); the author stresses that the phonemic status of the tonal vs metrical phenomena is not yet established for any variety.

readall_conflicts: The catalog codes 'Cora' as fixed-strict antepenultimate (Gordon 2002, resting on Preuss 1912 'Sehr häufig fällt er auf die drittletzte Silbe', a tendency statement for Jesús María Cora). this disagrees with any fixed: antepenultimate syllable coding of Cora and sides with the on-file El Nayar statements of Kim & Valdovinos 2014 (Mariteco: lexical, initial and final stress both found in disyllables) and Casad 1984 (phonemic tone partly independent of stress). McMahon 1967 remains unread (all copies gated), so it neither confirms nor resolves the disagreement. The one work opened (Casad 1984 in Langacker ed. 1984, Jesús María dialect) conflicts in type with the catalog's Gordon record: Gordon codes Cora as fixed antepenultimate stress, while Casad states that tone is phonemic, that stress has primary and secondary degrees operating partly independently of tone, and describes high-tone placement as lexical and morphologically mobile (tone attraction, number- and tense/aspect-conditioned shifts), giving no fixed stress position; penultimate (not antepenultimate) stress is mentioned only as an earlier-stage rule behind some tone shifts. Part of the discrepancy may be dialectal/analytical: Gordon's source (McMahon 1967) is on Presidio de los Reyes Cora, Casad's on Jesús María. The Jáuregui 2025 thesis (Tereseño Cora) could not be opened, so it adds nothing either way.

audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant (antepenult default in 3+ syllables / initial in disyllables, with lexically marked exceptions; not in the strict set), with a caution note that Casad 1984 and Kim & Valdovinos 2014 treat stress as lexical with tone/laryngealization interactions — 'lexical' or 'conflict' if the catalog requires the modern description to govern.
audit.reasoning: Quote: verified verbatim in the now-held Preuss 1912 text at the cited pages. Source quality: the classification 'fixed-strict, dominant, antepenult' rests on a database pattern (StressTyp -> Gordon 2002) whose cited source (Casad 1984, held and read) gives no positional rule, backed up by a 1912 transcription-convention note that itself hedges ('sehr häufig', acute-marked exceptions, double-peaked words, fluctuating accent). sources.quote: Instrumental pilot study of the same Jesús María (Mariteco) variety Preuss described. Treats Cora as having 'lexical stress' (following Casad n.d.); 'Disyllables introduce the dimension of stress to the analysis. Initial stress and final stress are both found. Counts for monomorphemic disyllables in isolation: younger speaker 28 initial-stressed vs 22 final-stressed (of 50); older speaker 30 initial vs 37 final (of 67). The definite prefix ɨ- attracts stress off the noun. No tonal contrast
